title: How to Visit the Sick and the Dying
subtitle: A pastor's guide to hospital visitation, bedside ministry, praying with the dying, and being present in the room where everything is at stake

sections.title: The Hospital Chair
sections.body:
There is a chair in every hospital room, pushed against the wall, vinyl and cold. You will spend a good part of your ministry in that chair. No one writes about it. No conference is built around it. But it is where a large share of the real work of a pastor gets done.

Walk in slow. Lower your voice. The room has its own gravity, and you must enter it on its terms, not yours.

The sick person is not at home in this room and neither are you, which is good, because it means you arrive as a fellow stranger and not as an expert. You are not there to perform a visit. You are there to be with a person who is afraid, who is bored, who is humiliated by a gown that does not close, who has not been truly seen by anyone in white coats all day. Pull the chair close. Sit where they can see your face without turning their neck. Then stay long enough that they know you did not come to check a box.

sections.title: What to Do Before You Go In
sections.body:
Find out what you are walking into before you push the door open. A new diagnosis is a different room than a recovery. A dying man needs something other than a man getting a knee replaced.

Know the name. Know the situation. Know whether the family is present and whether they are at war with each other in the waiting room.

Then empty your hands. Do not arrive with an agenda longer than a few minutes, because the sick tire quickly and a long visit is a burden disguised as a kindness. Leave your phone in the car or silenced and pocketed, never glanced at. Wash your hands at the door so they see you did. And ask a nurse, quietly, whether now is a good time, because there is no ministry in interrupting a bath or a hard procedure. The smallest courtesies preach. They tell the patient that you took them seriously enough to think ahead.

sections.title: What to Actually Do at the Bedside
sections.body:
Most of bedside ministry is listening. You ask how they are and then you let them answer, the real answer, not the one they give the nurse. You do not rush to reassure. You do not turn their fear into a teaching moment.

Touch them if they will let you. A hand on the arm, a hand held. Sickness makes a body feel untouchable, and a steady human hand says otherwise.

Read a short passage, slowly, something old and known. The twenty-third Psalm has carried more dying saints than any sermon ever preached. Then pray, but pray briefly and pray for what they actually want, which you will only know because you asked. Do not pray a sermon over a tired person. Pray the way you would speak to a friend with the door of heaven open. And before you leave, tell them when you will come again, and then come, because the second visit is the one that proves the first was not a performance.

sections.title: When They Are Dying
sections.body:
The room of the dying is different, and you must not pretend it is not. There comes a point where everyone in the room knows, and the cruelest thing you can do is keep up a bright pretense that wastes the hours that are left.

Do not lie to a dying person. Do not promise a recovery you cannot promise. The dying have a clarity the living lack, and false cheer insults it.

What they need is permission and presence. Permission to speak about what is coming, if they want to. Presence that does not flinch when they do. Ask them if they are afraid, and then be able to sit with the answer. Help them say the things that must be said to the people who must hear them, the I love you and the I forgive you and the forgive me, because deathbeds are where families are healed or wounded for a generation. Pray the great old words of the faith over them, the ones that do not depend on their being able to respond. And when speech is gone, stay anyway. Hearing is the last sense to leave. Read Scripture to a person who can no longer answer. They are still in the room. So be in it with them.

sections.title: What You Carry Out of the Room
sections.body:
You will walk out of these rooms and into a parking garage and sit in your car for a minute before you can drive. That minute is not weakness. It is the honest cost of having been truly present.

You cannot do this work and feel nothing. If you feel nothing, you have started going through motions, and the sick can smell a man going through motions from across the room.

So let it cost you, and then do not carry it alone. Tell God what you saw. Tell one trusted friend what it took out of you. Do not let the accumulation of other people's worst days harden into a shell that lets you visit without being moved. The goal is not to become unmoved. The goal is to remain tender and keep going, which is only possible if you are being tended yourself. I have left rooms I will never forget, and the only reason I could enter the next one was that I let the last one matter. A shepherd who has stopped grieving has stopped shepherding. Go to the bedside. Stay in the chair. Then go and be held, so there is still a whole person to send next time.
